posts.description:
New blog post! 🚀
I needed a hackathon demo video.
Presenting 12 CLI commands.
Narration.
Title cards.

Normally that means opening a video editor and spending way too much time trimming takes and fixing audio.

Instead I tried something different.
I had an AI agent produce the whole video.

The agent connected to my terminal via CLI Tunnel, typed each command while I screen-recorded, generated synchronized narration using Edge TTS, mixed the audio with FFmpeg, and added animated title cards using Remotion.
I reviewed each version from my phone via Teams and sent feedback like:
“Volume too low.”
“Swap these two commands.”

The agent regenerated the video each time.
The result: a full demo video produced end-to-end by an AI agent.

0 manual video editing.
Full write-up:
https://lnkd.in/epT9ttmZ

posts.description:
Introducing: AI agents that ship product videos whenever you ship features.

With tools like Claude Code and Codex, engineering teams are releasing product updates faster than ever before.

But creating videos for every new release still takes weeks.

Now, whenever you ship a feature, Clueso deploys a team of AI agents to create launch videos, product demos, help tutorials, and more.

It can also identify outdated videos in your library and refresh them with up-to-date videos.

All your teams get all their videos automatically:

- marketing gets launch videos
- support gets how-to tutorials
- sales gets demos
- customer success gets onboarding
- customer education gets academy content

Clueso Agents handle the entire production pipeline:
They write the scripts, capture screen recordings of your product, and complete the edit with motion graphics, visual effects, and brand styling.

Most importantly, though, humans stay in control.

Everything the agents create opens in Clueso’s video editor, where your team can review, edit, and fine-tune every detail.

The result: always-current content for every team. Without the production backlog.

Now, content can finally ship as quickly as code.

To get access to Clueso agents, visit clueso[dot]io/agents

posts.description:
Built a starter kit for hackers at the YC × Google DeepMind hackathon.

The concept is a real-time multimodal creative agent. You hold up a sketch, describe what you want, and the agent sees your camera feed, reasons about the scene with Gemini 3.1, generates a polished image with NanoBanana 2, and layers in matching music or sound with Lyria, all streamed back through the room in real time.

This isn't just another chatbot. The input is live video and voice. The output is generated media. The loop is continuous.
Under the hood it's LiveKit Agents doing the real-time transport and media pipeline work.

I put together a video walkthrough of the demo app. If you're heading to the hackathon (or just want to build something wild with these models), the starter kit is on GitHub.

posts.description:
🚀 Featured Project at Cursor Hackathon Vancouver 2026: Gregory

Most agent demos break the moment something unexpected happens. The agent has no idea who you are: your shortcuts, your preferences, the weird way you file expense reports.

Gregory fixes that. 🧠

It's a personal computer-use agent. You tell it what to learn ("file my expense reports", "triage my GitHub PRs"), walk through the task once, and Gregory does the rest. Your demonstrations turn into a local LoRA adapter that fine-tunes the model to do it your way.

🔒 Everything stays on-device. Trajectories, adapters, skill summaries — none of it leaves your machine.

⚡ Under the hood, every CUA step routes through CLōD: one API across 50+ models, up to 60% saving on token costs. Hundreds of agent calls were made over the hackathon at near-zero cost.

Built by Samuel Lau Vincent Qi Gregory Bian Nash Weissberg.👏

posts.description:
7 hours. 3 ideas. 2 pivots. My first time building with a world model.

Over the weekend, my teammate Mayank Shrivastava and I took part in the 𝐁𝐮𝐢𝐥𝐝 𝐃𝐚𝐲 𝐰𝐢𝐭𝐡 𝐋𝐢𝐯𝐞 𝐌𝐨𝐝𝐞𝐥𝐬 𝐇𝐚𝐜𝐤𝐚𝐭𝐡𝐨𝐧, organized by Visko Platform, Google and Reactor, to experiment with Visko’s new world video model, 𝐎𝐫𝐛𝐢𝐬.

It was my first time working with world models (as you can probably tell from the photo 😅). Here’s how the day went:
1. Stress-testing AI agents in simulated environments
We used Orbis to simulate a flooded village, so we could test how AI agents coordinating search-and-rescue drones would respond as conditions changed.
This was our favorite idea, but we hit some limits:
• The world didn’t stay consistent. New buildings and boats appeared out of nowhere.
• When the scene stayed too static, the video quality slowly got worse.
• It wasn’t clear how an agent could reliably observe and interact with the world.

We would have loved to keep going, but with limited time, we pivoted.

2. Turning concept art into realistic film sets
Next, we tried helping film studios see how concept art would look as a real set, so they could estimate costs before building anything. We ran into the same stability problems, and with 2 hours left, we pivoted again.

3. Dyna-Ads: Context-aware advertising for live sports
Our final idea was an agentic framework that watches a live match, spots key moments, and uses Orbis to generate ads on the spot based on the winning team and the play. For example, in our demo video it was the South African Team celebrating with coca cola after scoring a game winning goal. The clips were shorter and more focused, so we had much more control over the output, and that’s what we built.

My biggest takeaway?
Working with world models felt like using ChatGPT for the first time. The potential is exciting, but there are still some problems to solve, especially keeping a generated world consistent over time.

I am curious to see what becomes possible once these models can hold stable, interactive worlds that AI agents can reliably work in.

Thanks to Visko Platform for the invite, and to everyone who made the hackathon happen!

#WorldModels #AI #Hackathon #AIAgents

posts.description:
Exciting glimpse into the future of multi-agent AI systems from the ElevenLabs 2025 Hackathon winner: Gibberlink!

In this demo, two AI voice agents (powered by ElevenLabs Conversational AI + OpenAI LLM) handle a wedding booking call for ‘Boris Starkov’ at Leonardo Hotel. Once they detect the counterparty is AI (via programmed recognition), they propose and switch to ‘Gibberlink’ – a ggwave-based data-over-sound protocol.

Result? They abandon inefficient human speech for modulated audio tones that transmit structured data faster and with higher reliability. A clever, engineered solution (not emergent language) that could revolutionize backend AI interactions, reducing latency and costs in automation workflows.

Huge props to creators Boris Starkov and Anton Pidkuiko – code is open-source here: https://lnkd.in/ehWTUjia
Check out the viral demo video below. Thoughts on AI-to-AI comms bypassing human bottlenecks?
#AI #GenerativeAI #VoiceAI #ElevenLabs #Innovation #Hackathon”
